title: Dawn in Boon.land
logline: At dawn, Boof digs a warm egg out of a frozen furrow — an unspent wish, humming like a held breath, that every map in Boon.land refuses to write down.
epigraph: A wish is not a thing. It is a direction the world has not agreed to turn yet.
description: Chapter 1 of Lore.Land: Dawn in Boon.land. Boof—a dog who works for the land and trusts an honest scent—unearths a warm egg in a frozen furrow: an unspent wish a genie never finished granting, which the maps cannot hold because it has not happened yet.

content.text: Dawn smelled of {{dawn-smell}}. Boof put her nose to the ground and read the field the way she read it every morning: loam-dark under the rime, burr-rough along the fence-foot.

variants: rime and the miller's first fire
frost and the last of the night's rain

content.text: Everything was where it belonged. The latch lifted at the kitchen. The bucket knocked the well. A blackbird tried the same few notes until one pleased it. Beneath the berry rows, the torch-ants kept their little hearths, and their patient magic warmed the roots through winter; above them, the boonberries slept under ice, each holding a drop of light.

On the coldest nights, when the frost split a furrow, you could see the hearths at work: a pin of light no bigger than a seed, carried down along a root by something with more legs than Boof cared to count, and behind it another, and another, a whole small procession going home along streets no map had room for. Boof did not dig. Some business is not a dog's, and the ants had never once asked her for anything.

Torch-ants were businesslike, and very particular about torches. If one went out at the wrong corner, the whole street stopped until it was relit from the right one. Children lay with an ear to the frost to hear them keeping their corners: a dry, small ticking, like seeds in a gourd.

Boof followed the rows past the fence that leaned into last year's weeds, past the scraping-post where the miller knocked the loam off his boots. She sniffed a root here and there, and the field gave back its usual answers: {{field-answers}}.

content.text: Boof knew this field. She worked for the land, wherever the fences stood. Nobody paid her, and nobody had needed to; the land kept her the way it kept the ants, without either side signing anything. She did not especially like blueberries. She appreciated them, which is a different thing, and which the field seemed to know.
She sniffed. Stepped. Stopped. One furrow was warm. Too warm. Beneath it, the ants had stopped working. Or not stopped — gathered, the way they gather at a hearth when a new coal is laid.
Boof dug. First frost, then soft earth, then a little cloud of steam. At the bottom lay an egg the size of a curled cat, dark as an old lamp.
She touched it with one paw. It hummed.

The steam climbed past her ears, met the cold, and came down as snow that did not sting, because it was warm. Children have a name for warm snow, and a way of making it they explain only to other children: a hearth-drift. Nobody had taught the field how.

Down the walls of the hole, the torch-ants were already at their business. Her digging had cut one of their streets clean through. They did not complain; they carried their torches around the break in single file, a detour of pinpricks bending across the shell. One stopped and held its torch against the egg, the way a lamplighter tests a wick, then went back down a shade brighter.
No nest. No tracks. No mother-scent. She went around the hole once more, slowly. Whatever had brought it here had left no way to follow.
Inside the shell, an unspent wish waited. Boof heard only the hum.

content.text: Ant-warmth smelled earthy and even, like bread left under a cloth. This was sharper. A candle just blown out. Boof knew the paths to the kitchens, the mill with its flour-pale doorstep, and the grove nobody liked to name after dark; after supper people said the downhill trees, as if the grove might hear its name and come up to see what was wanted. She had never found an egg on any of them. Certainly not one that warmed a whole furrow.
She rested her chin on the rim of the hole. The egg hummed against the earth. Under her chin, she felt it answer.
She would have preferred a trail. Trails usually ended with something you could eat: a dropped crust, a vole, once a whole wheel of cheese gone into the ditch to think things over.
Every boonberry had been a blueberry once. A wish had passed over it on the way to being granted, leaving a little of its light behind. Most slept through everything: snow, crows, harvest.

The town used them for supper and lanterns: berry-lamps in {{lamp-jars}}, crust-gold pies at harvest. Nobody ate one warm. By the time a boonberry reached a table it had given its light to a lamp or a pie, and what was left was sweet and ordinary. Boof had never wondered what the light was for. She had been busy.

content.text: The berry nearest the egg shed its frost. A gold seam opened in its skin with a small sound, like a thumbnail on a jar lid. Its light leaned toward the shell, then past it, down the slope.

The next berry turned. Then the next. Frost slid off the leaves in glass-clear sheets and broke on the furrows like a tray of cups set down too fast. Row by row, a low glow led toward the grove. Boof followed with her nose. The berries remembered this hum. Long ago, it had passed them going the other way.
She looked back at the hole. Something had come home. Why had nobody come to fetch it?

content.text: Before the frost was off the fences, Boof had carried the egg to the map-house in an old feed-sack. It was warm as a loaf and considerably heavier. She set it on the reading table. The archivist fetched a book.

The map-house smelled of {{reading-room-smell}}. Along the back wall ran the drying-line, where new maps hung by their corners like washing over a slate trough. In a loaf-wide gap between rolled maps in the rafters, a young shelf-owl sat as if it had been shelved there.
Along a fold in the map, two roads touched. Boof knew those roads. A day's walk lay between them. Outside, a cart bell rang beneath the window.
The archivist smoothed the fold. The bell dwindled to a far, thin chime. “Leave room for the path,” he murmured, to the map or to the bell, and did not say which path.
Boof lifted her head. The archivist put a press-stone on the crease. Neither looked away first.
His press-stones sat along the table's lip, river-flat, six in a rack cut for seven. One is always missing; it is the first thing an apprentice learns and the last thing anybody finds.

Then he tried to enter the egg in the book. First, as archivists do, he pencilled it small in the margin in the makers' old shorthand, to see whether it would bear ink: .[egg], a thing that stays where it is put. The pencil skidded. He rubbed it out and tried ~[egg], a thing still on its way. That one held, faint as a hair.
So he dipped the pen. Egg, one. Dawnward field. Unclaimed. The ink gathered into beads and rolled off the page.
He tried a second pen, and then the good steel nib he kept for boundary disputes. Boof waited.
Maps keep what has happened. An unspent wish has not happened yet, and the page had nowhere to put it.

At last he pegged the page on the drying-line, since a stubborn entry sometimes sets when nobody is watching. The beads ran down and dropped into the trough until the page hung clean as a washed collar, all but the pencilled tilde. Below, the ink sat in one black drop and would not mix with the water.

He unpegged the page and laid it in the book beside the old field map: an ordinary field, in some long-dead surveyor's brown ink. “First ink stays,” he said. Nobody scrapes the first hand on a map; whatever comes after goes in pencil beside it, so whoever opens the book next can see what changed, and what it changed from. Beside the ordinary field, faint as a hair, the tilde waited.
The archivist wiped the table. Boof watched the stone. That, at least, he had known how to hold down.

content.text: Outside, the berries still leaned toward the grove, every row combed one way like wet fur. Boof had spent the morning asking a book. The field had been pointing all along.

She settled the feed-sack against her chest, where a pup might ride. A fine gold crack had opened at the egg's crown. It looked like a door left slightly ajar. The hum kept its steady measure. Her paws found another.

Down the slope. Past the fogged cold-frames, past the last row, to the sloe hedge where the field gave up being a field. There she paused. Behind her stood a house full of maps. Ahead lay the way the berries remembered.
She went ahead.

content.text: Evening laid long light across the field. Boof was hungry; somewhere uphill a kitchen was {{supper-smell}}, and the smell followed her like a dog that had not been told to stay. The egg was warm. For a while, that was all. Behind her, the berries glowed under their leaves. Ahead, the first trees crowded close.

variants: roasting the last of the parsnips

content.text: Then a sound came out of the grove. HONK.
Long, bent, and rather pleased with itself. Like a goose that had learned jazz. Boof stopped with one paw raised. The egg's hum slipped into time with it.

High over the treeline, nine geese crossed the last light in a ragged, swinging line and answered, each honk a little behind where a sensible goose would put it. Jazz-geese, people called that kind, and shut their windows.
She waited for a second note from the grove. Leaves stirred. Nothing more.
She put her paw down and entered the trees.

loreItems.description: Boof is a dog based on Spwashi's dog. She works for the land, not an owner—paid in blueberries, honest scents, and trails that end in something real. Her wants are small, and small wants are the hardest magic.

Boonberries are blueberries a wish once passed over. Each holds a drop of the granting; they wake when they remember being wished over. They grow in cold weather only because ants warm the soil beneath them with a small, patient magic—the ant-hearths, a warmth the town spends without naming.
The egg is an unspent wish—the last item in the ledger of a Discount Genie who closed his practice. Its hum is a held breath: a sentence stopped one word before the wishing word.
Boon.land's records hold only what has happened. An ungranted wish has not happened yet, so ink beads off the page; the maps end where its hum begins.
The field remembers a direction before the people do—the berries lean toward the grove, the way a granting once went.
A hairline crack shaped like a door left ajar opens along the egg's crown as it warms. Something inside is waiting to be finished, not hatched.
The grove downhill keeps echoes and will not be named after dark; Boof carries the wish toward it. (Chamber 02.)
At dusk, one far-off HONK rises from the treeline—one note, like a goose that learned jazz. It is a signature, though no one has met the signer yet.

Torch-ants keep the field's lit streets along the berry roots all winter. They are businesslike and particular about torches: one that goes out at the wrong corner stops the whole street until it is relit from the right one. When Boof's digging cut a street, they detoured around the break, and one tested its torch against the egg like a lamplighter testing a wick, and went home brighter.

The map-house hangs new maps on a drying-line over a slate trough; an entry that will not take ink drips back into the trough and sits there unmixed. Its press-stones live in a rack cut for seven that holds six — one is always missing. A young owl roosts in a loaf-wide gap in the rafters.

Archivists pencil an entry small in the margin, in the makers' old shorthand, before they ink it, to see whether it will bear. The egg would not take .[egg], a thing that stays where it is put; it held only ~[egg], a thing still on its way.
Steam from the warm furrow fell back as warm snow — what children call a hearth-drift, and make by a method they explain only to other children. The field made one by itself.

First ink stays: the map-house never scrapes the first hand on a map. Whatever comes after goes in pencil beside it, so the next reader can see what changed and what it changed from. The egg's only entry is a pencilled tilde beside an ordinary field.

table.place: The dawnward field at first light: frost-skinned berry rows, a fence leaning into last year's weeds, the miller's scraping-post, and one furrow steaming where it ought to be iron-hard. Lie with an ear to the rime and you can hear the torch-ants keeping their corners underneath, a dry ticking like seeds in a gourd. Uphill, the map-house: oak-gall ink and cold slate, new maps pegged on the drying-line like washing, a rack of press-stones cut for seven that holds six, and a young owl shelved in the rafters. Downhill, past the sloe hedge, the grove nobody names after dark.
table.light: Grey dawn over white frost, the only warm light leaking up out of the ground; high, dusty window-light in the map-house by mid-morning; and by evening a long amber that leaves the berry rows glowing under their leaves like banked coals, every one of them leaning the same way.

hooks: The seventh press-stone. The archivist has decided this is the year, and would like help he will not quite ask for: rumour says the stone was carried off long ago to hold down something that would not lie flat. Follow it through kitchens, the mill and the ditch — and when it comes home, notice which of the other six has gone missing.

A dark corner. A torch went out at the wrong corner overnight and a whole ant-street has stopped; one berry row is freezing through, and the frost is feeling its way toward the miller's cellar. The ants will not take a light from a lantern, a candle or a well-meaning stranger. Find the right corner, on streets no map has room for, and wait to be allowed.

A boundary that will not take ink. Two neighbours bring a fence dispute to the map-house, and the good steel nib the archivist keeps for boundary disputes takes only one of their lines; the other beads off the page and drops into the trough. Something one of them is claiming has not happened yet. Find out what, before it does.
encounters: Children lying with their ears to the rime shush you hard: an ant-street is ticking under your boots, and one careless step puts a corner out.

Steam off a warm furrow meets the cold and comes down as snow that does not sting. The children call it a hearth-drift and will explain the method only to another child; one of you will have to be one, convincingly.

A scent-trail through the rows — vole, frost-bitten clover, the sour ghost of a fox who thought better of it — ends at a whole wheel of cheese gone into the ditch to think things over. Somebody is missing a cheese and will want to know who found it.

A cart bell rings under the map-house window while a map lies folded on the table; for as long as it rings, two roads a day's walk apart lie touching along the crease, and the archivist reaches for a press-stone.
The young shelf-owl in the rafters will not let anyone shelve a rolled map in its loaf-wide gap. It is keeping the space for something nobody has written yet, and says so with its beak.
At dusk nine jazz-geese cross the last light in a ragged, swinging line, each honk a little behind the beat. Every window on the lane shuts. In the downhill trees, something answers once.

finds.use: Follow the brightest torch-ant: they test their torches against anything warm and unfinished and go home a shade brighter, so a bright one has just come from something worth finding. The catch: cut a street and they detour without complaint, but a torch out at the wrong corner stops the whole street, and a stopped street is a frozen row by morning.

Peg a page on it and leave the room. An entry that is so will set while nobody watches; one that has not happened yet beads off and drops into the trough, unmixed. The catch: it tells you only that a thing is not yet so, never what it will be — and the archivist counts his pegs.

Borrowed from the rack, one holds flat anything that keeps curling: a map, a letter, an argument somebody keeps unfolding. The catch: the rack is cut for seven and holds six; take one and it holds five, and the archivist knows before you reach the door.

bracework.does: A window the size of a page. Look in and you see the map as the field sees it: every ant-street, scent-trail and leaning row drawn in, for as long as you can hold your breath.
bracework.costs: Perspective changes both sides a little. The map keeps one line it cannot account for, which the archivist must pencil beside the first ink, never over it; the row that did the watching forgets for a day which way it was leaning. And the torch-ants will want to know whose warmth you borrowed.

table.question: When a berry leans its light toward one of you instead of toward the grove, what unfinished thing are you carrying?
